class LRUCache:
    """
    Least Recently Used (LRU) Cache with O(1) get and put operations.

    The cache maintains a doubly linked list to track the order of usage,
    where the most recently used item is at the head and the least recently
    used item is at the tail. A dictionary maps keys to nodes for O(1) lookup.

Before the press, scientific knowledge was fragile, localized, and prone to corruption through manual copying errors. The printing press fundamentally altered this landscape by enabling the mass production of identical texts, thereby standardizing information and facilitating the rapid dissemination of ideas across Europe.

One of the most profound impacts was the stabilization of data. In the manuscript era, every copy of a text introduced new errors, making it difficult for scholars to build reliably upon previous work. With printed books, scientists could reference the same page numbers, diagrams, and numerical tables with confidence. This standardization allowed for precise comparison and verification of results across different regions. For instance, astronomical tables and anatomical illustrations could be reproduced with fidelity, enabling researchers in Italy to critique or expand upon findings from Germany without the distortion inherent in hand-copied versions.

Furthermore, the press democratized access to knowledge. Previously, scientific texts were expensive luxury items confined to monasteries and wealthy patrons. The reduction in cost and increase in availability meant that a broader class of literate individuals—including merchants, artisans, and minor clergy—could engage with scientific ideas. This expanded audience created a feedback loop where authors had to write more clearly and logically to appeal to non-specialists, fostering a culture of clarity and empirical observation over obscure scholasticism.

The printing press also accelerated the pace of scientific debate and correction. Errors could be identified and corrected in subsequent editions, creating a dynamic process of peer review long before formal journals existed. This rapid exchange allowed for the swift spread of revolutionary ideas, such as those of Copernicus, Vesalius, and later Newton. The ability to print diagrams was particularly crucial; visual representation became a central tool of scientific argumentation, allowing complex mechanical or biological structures to be understood universally.

Ultimately, the printing press shifted science from a static preservation of ancient authorities to a dynamic, collaborative process. It created a shared intellectual infrastructure that allowed discoveries to accumulate rather than disappear. By ensuring that knowledge was permanent, accessible, and verifiable, the press laid the essential groundwork for the Scientific Revolution, transforming individual insights into a collective, progressive body of human understanding.
